html:
The Vai syllabary is a script for the Vai language of Liberia and Sierra Leone, made in the 1830s by Momolu Duwalu Bukele. It is one of the few writing systems invented in modern Africa that took hold, and it is still used.

Bukele said the signs came to him in a dream. Each sign stands for a syllable rather than a single sound, which suits Vai well. The script spread quickly: Vai people taught it to each other, outside any school or church, and used it for letters, accounts, records and later translations of the Quran and the Bible.

It was the first of a wave of new African scripts, including the Bamum script of Cameroon and N'Ko for the Manding languages. It is often compared to the Cherokee syllabary, made in the 1820s by Sequoyah. The Vai script was added to the Unicode standard in 2008.
